scope: Independent analysis of the 21 October 2026 OpenBox developer meeting only

evidence_scale.strong: Direct statement corroborated by a clear on-screen artifact, or multiple consistent direct statements
evidence_scale.moderate: Clear direct statement without independent corroboration, or internal artifact not operationally verified
evidence_scale.limited: Second-hand, ambiguous, future-contingent, or ASR-sensitive statement

entries.claim: OpenBox presents itself as a runtime governance and attestation platform for AI agents.
entries.caveat: Architecture/positioning was shown; runtime behavior was not demonstrated.

entries.claim: The proposed open-core split opens the PEP and verdict/attestation format while retaining decision, administration/control, identity/risk and verification services as proprietary value.
entries.caveat: License and timing were still under review.

entries.claim: PEP release gates include interface stability, decoupling, secret scrubbing, security policy, conformance tests and fail-closed behavior.
entries.caveat: Completion was not established.

entries.claim: An internal inventory asserts 87 features across nine areas: 62 live on main, five live with caveats, four staging/own repo, and 16 on feature branches.
entries.caveat: No features were independently tested.

entries.claim: The team decided to productize the broad platform into understandable products/sub-brands organized around user and problem.
entries.caveat: The product taxonomy was due after the meeting and not final.

entries.claim: OpenBox Gate is the proposed first product wedge: local policy enforcement for coding-agent tool calls with approvals and verifiable proof.
entries.caveat: The terminal interaction in the mockup is labeled illustrative.

entries.claim: The commercial thesis is free individual use, then paid Team and Enterprise controls; a displayed Team price of about $15/seat/month is explicitly a placeholder.
entries.caveat: No willingness-to-pay, margin, conversion or retention evidence was presented.

entries.claim: Billing was incomplete and explicitly prevented prior monetization; Gate plus billing was targeted for the end of the following week.
entries.caveat: No implementation status or release test was shown.

entries.claim: A Vietnamese development-house general manager reportedly fears cross-client leakage by developers and their tools and is seeking controls.
entries.caveat: The customer was not present; buying process and willingness to pay were not established.

entries.claim: Engineering said existing technology could address that dev-house problem, but more work was needed to provide a direct solution.
entries.caveat: Required work was not decomposed.

entries.claim: Only two named external organizations were reported to have tried getting the system running.
entries.caveat: Names are ASR-sensitive; attempts are not equivalent to production use or payment.

entries.claim: One external setup received a custom SDK built in roughly a week; the other remained in SDK/Cloudflare troubleshooting and was awaiting a reply.
entries.caveat: Production status, usage and commercial terms were not shown.

entries.claim: Existing integrations/relationships had not converted into traction, and referral analytics were not available without tagged links.
entries.caveat: No analytics system was inspected.

entries.claim: The immediate revenue target was phrased as showing one million ARR within a quarter ending around January.
entries.evidence_type: direct statement verified by second ASR pass
entries.caveat: No pipeline or price-volume model supported it.

entries.claim: The proposed viral channel includes paying developers/influencers to review Gate and provide testimonials, with suggested spend from $100 to $10,000.
entries.evidence_type: direct proposal verified by second ASR pass
entries.caveat: Disclosure rules, editorial independence and success metrics were not discussed.

entries.claim: A paid directory/repository placement at $150/month for three months was proposed as a pilot.
entries.caveat: Attribution and success thresholds were not stated.

entries.claim: The first seed cohort would be recruited manually through every employee's network, targeting one developer in a credible company per week.
entries.evidence_type: direct plan verified by second ASR pass
entries.caveat: Network-sourced trial is useful for learning but is not evidence of organic demand.

entries.claim: A participant required a designed onboarding experience: concierge support, one narrow use case, fast installation, and immediate visible proof/audit playback.
entries.evidence_type: direct challenge verified by second ASR pass
entries.caveat: No task-level owner, metric or test plan was recorded.

entries.claim: The team wanted roughly 40 people it could call users in November while acknowledging it did not yet have usage-depth metrics.
entries.evidence_type: direct statement verified by second ASR pass
entries.caveat: A login/installation threshold is materially weaker than retained or outcome-producing use.

entries.claim: Product owners were proposed for each offer, spanning page, marketing, customer feedback and backlog; another participant challenged conflating product management with sales and questioned staffing capacity.
entries.caveat: The proposal was partly reframed as a future-state organization.

entries.claim: Tahir is named owner of the developer GTM plan and sets most near-term priorities and deadlines in the meeting.
entries.caveat: This meeting alone cannot establish the company's general decision model.

entries.claim: Watermarking/fingerprinting was considered for productization as IP governance, but its repeatability versus bespoke-project status remained unresolved.
entries.caveat: Customer name and timing are ASR-sensitive; no generalized demand evidence was presented.

entries.claim: Security language was judged more compelling and better funded than governance for developers and managers.
entries.caveat: No message test, win/loss data or buyer study was presented.

entries.claim: Immediate outputs were a final product taxonomy/sub-brands, website, tactical plans and ownership by early November.
entries.caveat: The meeting did not present a sequenced, capacity-based product roadmap.
